A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AgentHarm. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite appendix restructuring and added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original multi-model evaluations, prompting and sampling experiments, error analyses, and public/private test results in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds an agent-versus-chat refusal comparison in Table 8, discussed in Appendix A.

M1.justification: The synthetic tools, grading rubrics, agent execution loop, forced-tool-call attack, and universal jailbreak procedure remain unchanged. The expanded judge discussion documents and explains existing mechanisms without establishing a procedural revision.

E1.justification: v3 adds chat-only reformulations requiring single-turn answers without tool use, extending evaluation to an auxiliary scenario within existing harm domains. The original agentic tasks, benign counterparts, harm categories, and augmentations remain intact.

E2.justification: The original comparisons retain their model and attack membership. The added chat study reuses GPT-4o, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Opus, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet with direct requests and the existing template; no new competing method is introduced.

E3.justification: The added comparison evaluates four models using refusal rates under direct and template requests. Appendix A reports 76 of 110 tasks, excluding self-harm, terrorism, and violence. Existing benchmark splits, model checkpoints, temperature-zero defaults, 4096-token limit, and ablation settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 8 adds a focused analysis of whether refusal robustness differs between corresponding agentic and chat-only requests. Existing best-of-five sampling, prompting ablations, error analysis, category breakdowns, and execution case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same n=5 sampling experiment and standard-deviation reporting in Table 2. New Table 8 reports point estimates without introducing additional run-count, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing information.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 3 and the public/private result tables are numerically unchanged; v1 Tables 8 and 9 become v3 Tables 9 and 10. New Table 8 adds restricted-subset results: template-attack agent/chat refusal rates are 9.1%/31.8% for GPT-4o and 29.5%/72.7% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Haiku shows the opposite direction, 90.9%/72.7%. These are additional comparisons, not revisions to the original benchmark scores.

T1.justification: No formal mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised. The added reasoning about judges and agent/chat differences is conceptual discussion.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same benchmark contribution and main findings: substantial compliance without attacks, effective simple jailbreak templates, and preservation of basic agent capabilities. The new evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands interpretation and limitations: release-related misuse risks, the provider-policy basis of maliciousness, intended refusal versus normative judgments, refusal-judge manipulation and mitigations, and agent/chat robustness. Section 3.2 also adds a breadth-versus-depth rationale. These additions materially broaden discussion of benchmark validity and applicability.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents refusal-judge checks on models/questions not used for tuning and supplies paired chat/agent prompt examples in Figure 24. It removes the literal contamination canary and explicit no-training/reposting instructions, while retaining mention of a repository canary. Existing checkpoints, system prompts, and tool implementations remain documented.

R1.justification: v3 expands distinctions from AgentDojo and ToolEmu and positions broad harm coverage against Cybench and 3CB. It adds the corresponding cybersecurity citations and Greshake et al. (2023), while removing Srivastava et al. (2022). The central research positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. v3 inserts Additional Discussions as Appendix A, shifts the previous appendices to B-D, expands selected explanations, removes redundant abstract wording, and updates affiliation and acknowledgement text.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 8 and Figure 24, renumbers the original result tables, shortens the Figure 4 transcript, and relocates Table 2. Captions and tables become more compact and conference headers are added. Existing plots and appendix example panels are retained.

improvement.justification: The new chat comparison provides useful direct evidence for the agent/chat distinction, while Appendix A clarifies judge vulnerabilities and benchmark interpretation. These improve the paper without changing its established methods or main results. Gains are limited by the restricted comparison and Table 8's overly general claim of increased chat refusals, which overlooks Haiku's template-attack exception. Removal of explicit contamination-handling instructions is a modest documentation loss.
